Arctic grayling (Thymallus arcticus) is a freshwater salmonid widely distributed across Arctic and subarctic drainages of North America and Eurasia, exhibiting life-history traits shaped by short, cold growing seasons. A newly hatched alevin, still reliant on its yolk reserves, emerges from the gravel with a minimal body mass of approximately 0.0224 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0224 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 3.5 millimeters observed in this species. This modest neonatal mass underscores the severe energetic constraints faced by early life stages in high-latitude streams. The species grows steadily over several years, with individuals ultimately reaching a maximum total length of about 76 centimeters [Li = about 76 centimeters] in productive river systems. This ultimate size represents a significant investment of somatic growth before the onset of reproduction, a pattern common among iteroparous salmonids that must balance energy acquisition against the demands of an unpredictable environment.

Sexual maturation in Arctic grayling occurs when individuals have attained a total length of approximately 24 centimeters [Lp = approximately 24 centimeters], at which point they weigh roughly 148.3 grams [Wwp = roughly 148.3 grams] according to length-weight regressions derived from field-caught specimens. This size threshold is typically reached after three to five summers of growth, depending on local thermal regimes and food availability. The mass at this transitional stage reflects the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic costs of gamete production and spawning migrations. Comparative data from related salmonids suggest that this size at puberty is relatively modest, an adaptation likely tied to the short growing season and limited foraging opportunities in Arctic watersheds. Once mature, individuals invest substantially in annual reproductive bouts, although the precise timing of first spawning can vary considerably with latitude and environmental conditions.

The reproductive output of Arctic grayling is characterized by moderate fecundity and an annual spawning cycle typical of many iteroparous salmonids. Under the cool thermal conditions typical of its native habitat, specifically at a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], females produce on average 1,546 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 1,546 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately once per year [F_R_i = approximately once per year], yielding an annual reproductive output of over 35 eggs per day when calculated across the entire calendar year. This level of fecundity ensures that even with high egg and larval mortality rates, a sufficient number of offspring recruit into the population each year. The relatively large egg size, with a diameter of 3.5 millimeters, results in substantial yolk reserves that support the alevin through its critical first weeks of development. Temperatures above 7 °C [T = 7 °C] can accelerate embryonic development but also increase metabolic demands on the yolk-limited larvae.

Adult Arctic grayling are known for their striking dorsal fin and their preference for clear, cold rivers and lakes, where they feed primarily on aquatic invertebrates and, occasionally, on terrestrial insects that fall onto the water surface. The species demonstrates a remarkable capacity for growth over its lifetime, with the largest individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5,160 grams [Wwi = approximately 5,160 grams] in the most productive habitats. This maximum body mass, which corresponds to the previously mentioned total length of 76 centimeters, is attained only after many years of sustained feeding during the brief Arctic summers. Growth rates slow considerably following sexual maturation, as energy is increasingly diverted toward gamete production and the energetic costs of spawning migrations. Field studies have documented substantial variation in adult body mass among populations, with those in nutrient-rich systems achieving masses far exceeding those in oligotrophic tundra streams.

Longevity records for Arctic grayling indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions typical of northern rivers, which rarely exceed 7 °C [T = 7 °C] during the growing season. This extended lifespan, unusual among salmonids of comparable body size, is thought to reflect the low metabolic costs associated with cold-water residence and the species' relatively conservative reproductive strategy. Senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in growth rate and a reduction in reproductive output during the final years of life, rather than a catastrophic post-spawning mortality event. Populations in more southerly portions of the range may experience shorter lifespans due to higher metabolic demands and increased predation pressure, though direct comparative data remain sparse. The interplay between water temperature and longevity represents a critical axis of life-history variation requiring further investigation, particularly as climate change alters thermal regimes in Arctic ecosystems.
